questions.q: In Newtonian physics momentum is given by \(p = mv\) and is increased by applying a force, \(\Delta p = F\Delta t\). How does special relativity modify this so that an object cannot be accelerated beyond the speed of light?
options: It replaces the velocity \(v\) with the Lorentz factor \(\gamma\)
It replaces the mass \(m\) in the momentum formula with the relativistic mass, giving \(p = m_0 v / \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}\)
It removes the force term \(F\Delta t\) entirely
It makes momentum independent of velocity at high speed
questions.explanation: To calculate momentum in special relativity we replace \(m\) in the momentum formula with the relativistic mass, so \(p = m_0 v / \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}\). The momentum is consistent with a mass increase by a factor of gamma, \(m = \gamma m_0\), where \(m_0\) is the rest mass measured in a frame not moving relative to the object. The faster a body moves relative to the observer, the more massive it becomes.

questions.q: Calculate the relativistic momentum of a proton (rest mass \(m_0 = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\)) moving at \(0.6c\) relative to an observer.
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's worked example: substituting the rest mass and \(v = 0.6c\) into the relativistic momentum formula, the gamma factor \(1/\sqrt{1-0.6^2} = 1.25\) does the heavy lifting, giving \(3.76 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), larger than the Newtonian \(mv\).

questions.q: The equation \(E = mc^2\) expresses an equivalence of mass and energy. According to \(\Delta E = \Delta m c^2\), why do we usually not notice the increase in mass when we do work on an object?
options: Because energy and mass are completely unrelated quantities
Because the factor \(c^2 = 9 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\) is so large that it would take \(9 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{J}\) of energy to increase the mass by 1 kg
Because mass only changes during nuclear fission, never when ordinary work is done
Because the speed of light is too small to matter
questions.explanation: If we do work \(\Delta E\) on an object its mass will increase, but we do not notice this because of the factor \(c^2 = 9 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\). According to \(\Delta E = \Delta m c^2\) it would take \(9 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{J}\) to increase the mass by 1 kg. The same equivalence explains why the Sun and other stars generate energy by losing mass to nuclear fusion, and why fission reactors produce energy from a small loss of mass.

questions.q: From memory: state the equation expressing the equivalence of mass and energy, and outline two situations the textbook gives where mass is converted to energy.
keyPoints: The most famous equation, \(E = mc^2\), expresses an equivalence of mass and energy; if we do work \(\Delta E\) on an object its mass increases (\(\Delta E = \Delta m c^2\)).
The Sun and other stars generate their energy by losing mass to nuclear fusion.
Nuclear fission reactors produce electricity from the small loss of mass when large nuclei such as uranium-235 undergo fission.
The conversion factor is \(c^2 = 9 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\), so a tiny mass yields an enormous energy.
questions.explanation: The textbook stresses that \(E = mc^2\) is an equivalence of mass and energy, illustrated by the Sun losing mass to nuclear fusion and by fission reactors releasing energy from a small loss of mass. If you recalled the equation and at least two of these contexts, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Using \(m = m_0\gamma\), where \(m_0\) is the rest mass, why is it impossible for an object with mass to reach the speed of light?
options: Because at \(v = c\) the rest mass \(m_0\) falls to zero
Because if \(v = c\), \(\gamma\) becomes infinitely large, so an object travelling at \(c\) would have infinite mass, and speeds larger than \(c\) produce a negative value under the square root sign
Because the object would physically swell to an infinite size in its own frame
Because the relativistic mass becomes smaller than the rest mass
questions.explanation: The mass of an object increases as its velocity relative to an observer increases, given by \(m = m_0\gamma\). If \(v = c\), \(\gamma\) becomes infinitely large, so an object travelling at \(c\) would have infinite mass; speeds larger than \(c\) would produce a negative value under the square root sign, so these speeds are not possible. The rest mass \(m_0\) is the mass measured from a frame in the same inertial frame as the object.

questions.q: Calculate the mass increase of a proton that is accelerated from rest using 11 GeV of energy, an energy achievable in particle accelerators. (Take \(1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}\).)
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's worked example: convert 11 GeV to joules, then apply \(\Delta m = \Delta E/c^2\). The mass increase is \(1.96 \times 10^{-26}\,\mathrm{kg}\); since the proton's rest mass is \(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\), the accelerated proton behaves as though its mass is nearly 13 times its rest mass.

questions.q: In relativity, when more energy is given to a particle in a particle accelerator that is already approaching the speed of light, what does the energy mostly do?
options: It produces a large increase in speed and a small change in mass
It causes a large change in mass and only a small change in speed, because the particle gains inertia, so the speed cannot increase beyond the speed of light
It is radiated away as light, leaving the particle unchanged
It reduces the particle's rest mass so it can exceed the speed of light
questions.explanation: In relativity, when more energy is given to a particle approaching the speed of light, the energy causes a large change in mass and a small change in speed. By doing work on the particle it gains inertia, so the increase in energy has an ever-decreasing effect on the speed, which cannot increase beyond the speed of light no matter how much energy the particle is given. In particle accelerators every tiny increase in speed requires huge amounts of energy.

questions.q: In Newtonian physics, if a proton (rest mass \(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\)) were given 11 GeV of kinetic energy, what speed would the formula \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) predict, and why is this impossible?
working: This speed is not possible, as the maximum speed attainable is \(3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
questions.explanation: The textbook's sample problem: Newtonian physics predicts \(v = 1.45 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), almost five times the speed of light, which is impossible. This demonstrates the limitations of Newtonian physics; in reality the proton's energy goes into a mass increase, not an impossible speed.

questions.q: The episode uses the memory hook 'Stars, Smash, Smoke' for the three contexts where mass converts to energy. Which option correctly orders them from most to least mass converted?
options: Smoke (combustion) > Stars (fusion) > Smash (annihilation)
Smash (matter-antimatter annihilation, 100%) > Stars (fusion in the Sun, small fraction) > Smoke (combustion, negligible fraction)
Stars (fusion) > Smash (annihilation) > Smoke (combustion)
All three convert exactly the same fraction of mass
questions.explanation: Per the script, all three obey \(E = mc^2\) but differ wildly in efficiency: matter-antimatter annihilation converts 100% of the mass, nuclear fusion in the Sun converts a small but significant fraction, and ordinary combustion converts an utterly negligible fraction. That contrast in scale is itself an exam point.

questions.q: An electron and a positron, each of mass \(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), meet and annihilate, converting entirely to energy. Calculate the total energy released.
questions.explanation: Both masses convert entirely, so you must use two electron masses (using one would be out by a factor of two). Applying \(E = mc^2\) gives about \(1.64 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}\). This is the physics behind the PET scan, where positron-electron annihilation produces gamma rays.

questions.q: Explain why an object with mass cannot be accelerated to the speed of light. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: As an object's speed increases toward the speed of light, the Lorentz factor \(\gamma\) increases without limit, approaching infinity. Because the object's relativistic momentum equals \(\gamma m_0 v\) and its relativistic mass equals \(\gamma m_0\), both its momentum and its inertia increase without limit as it nears the speed of light. Accelerating it further therefore requires ever-increasing amounts of energy, and to actually reach the speed of light would require an infinite amount of energy, which is impossible. Hence no object with mass can be accelerated to the speed of light; only massless particles such as photons travel at exactly the speed of light.

criteria.descriptor: States that \(\gamma\) increases without limit (approaches infinity) as \(v \to c\).
Links this to relativistic momentum and mass also increasing without limit.
Concludes infinite energy would be required to reach \(c\), which is impossible.
Notes only massless particles (photons) travel at exactly \(c\).

questions.explanation: The band-six answer explains the mechanism (gamma runs to infinity, so mass and momentum run to infinity, so infinite energy is required) rather than just asserting the speed limit, and closes with the massless-photon contrast.
